nameStory: The 'ribseed' part of this plant's name comes from the distinctive ridged pattern on its tiny seeds, which look like they have ribs running along their surface. 'Sandmat' refers to its low-growing, mat-forming habit and its preference for sandy, disturbed soils where it spreads close to the ground.
description: Ribseed sandmat is a small, sprawling annual plant that hugs the ground in a flat mat. This tiny spurge rarely grows taller than a few inches, instead spreading outward with branching stems that can reach 6-12 inches across. Like all spurges, it has small, inconspicuous flowers and produces a milky white sap when broken. It's an uncommon visitor to New England, with only one recorded observation in the region.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: The tiny seeds have distinctive raised ribs or ridges running lengthwise, giving them a corrugated appearance that's visible with a hand lens

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a flat, spreading mat that stays very close to the ground, with stems radiating outward from the center

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves are arranged opposite each other along the stem and feel smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: Broken stems release a white, milky sap that may irritate skin - handle with care and wash hands afterward

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, greenish flowers lack petals and are easily overlooked - they sit in small clusters along the stems

habitat: In its native range, ribseed sandmat favors sandy, disturbed soils in open areas like roadsides, vacant lots, and waste places. In New England, it would most likely be found in similar disturbed habitats, possibly as an accidental introduction. Look for it in sandy soils with sparse vegetation where other plants struggle to establish.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as weather warms, and young plants begin their low-growing spread across bare soil.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their tiny, inconspicuous flowers throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: The distinctive ribbed seeds mature and are dispersed, while the annual plants begin to decline with cooler weather.
seasonality.winter: Dead plant material may persist, but this annual species survives only as seeds until the next growing season.

funFact: This little plant is such a rare visitor to New England that there's only been one confirmed sighting in the entire region - making it one of the most uncommon spurges you could possibly encounter on a nature walk!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small, mat-forming spurges like spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat. The key difference is in the seeds - ribseed sandmat's seeds have prominent lengthwise ribs, while spotted spurge has smooth seeds and prostrate sandmat has seeds with different surface textures.
contextualKnowledge: Like all spurges, ribseed sandmat belongs to the same family as poinsettias and produces that characteristic milky sap. The sap contains compounds that can cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals, so it's best to observe rather than handle these plants directly.
compareHints: Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name. While seaside sandmat also forms mats in sandy areas, it's found in coastal habitats and has different seed characteristics. Spotted spurge may look similar in growth habit but has the telltale red spot on each leaf and smooth seeds.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
